Italians were killed in the upheaval, some of them thrown into the karst sinkholes known as foibe, and a great many left Istria, Rijeka and Dalmatia in the years that followed; estimates of both the killings and the exodus differ considerably between sources. Italy established the Day of Remembrance by Law 92 of 30 March 2004, choosing 10 February because the Paris Peace Treaties, which transferred the territories, were signed on that date in 1947.
memorial_it_giorno_del_ricordo.traditions: A state ceremony is held at the Quirinal Palace in Rome, where the president addresses relatives of the victims and commemorative medals are presented to families. Wreaths are laid at the foiba of Basovizza near Trieste, the main national memorial, and mayors hold ceremonies in towns throughout the country. Schools devote lessons to the exodus, and exhibitions and concerts of remembrance are organised. It is a civil observance, not a day off work.
funFacts: The date recalls the signing of the Paris Peace Treaties on 10 February 1947.
Law 92 of 2004 also created a commemorative medal for relatives of the victims.
The foiba of Basovizza, near Trieste, serves as the principal national memorial site.

memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.intro: Japan observes 15 August as the day for mourning the war dead and praying for peace. It marks the announcement in 1945 that Japan would accept the Allied terms, bringing the Second World War to an end.
memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.history: On 15 August 1945 a recorded address by Emperor Hirohito, later known as the Jewel Voice Broadcast, was transmitted by radio, telling the public that the government had accepted the Potsdam Declaration. The formal instrument of surrender was signed aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September. The anniversary had long been observed informally when the Japanese cabinet gave it official standing in 1982 as a day for mourning the war dead and praying for peace.
memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.traditions: A national memorial ceremony is held at the Nippon Budokan in Tokyo, attended by the emperor and empress, the prime minister and relatives of the dead. At noon a minute of silence is observed across the country, marked by a siren or chime and broadcast live. Families visit graves and memorials, lanterns are floated on rivers in some regions, and broadcasters devote the day to accounts of the war years.
funFacts: The broadcast of 15 August 1945 was the first time most people in Japan had heard the emperor's voice.
In Japanese the day is called Shusen-kinenbi, the anniversary of the end of the war.
The formal surrender documents were signed later, on 2 September 1945, in Tokyo Bay.

memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.intro: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Day is observed in Japan on 6 August. It marks the atomic bombing of Hiroshima in 1945 and remembers those who died in the attack and later from its effects.
memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.history: An atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on the morning of 6 August 1945, destroying much of the city. Many people were killed at once and many more died afterwards from injuries and radiation; the full number is not precisely known. The first Peace Memorial Ceremony was held in 1947 by the then mayor, Shinzo Hamai, and the area near the point of detonation was rebuilt as the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park. The ceremony has since become the focus of the city's yearly appeal for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.traditions: The ceremony takes place at the Memorial Cenotaph in the Peace Memorial Park, with bereaved families, residents, national representatives and visitors from abroad present. At 8.15 in the morning, the moment of the detonation, the Peace Bell sounds and a minute of silent prayer is kept. A register listing those who have died is placed in the cenotaph, water and flowers are offered, doves are released and the mayor reads a Peace Declaration.
funFacts: The first Peace Memorial Ceremony was held in 1947, organised by the mayor of Hiroshima at the time, Shinzo Hamai.
The Peace Bell is rung at 8.15 in the morning, the time the bomb detonated over the city in 1945.
A register of the names of the dead is updated each year and placed inside the Memorial Cenotaph.

memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.intro: Nagasaki Peace Memorial Day is held on 9 August, the anniversary of the atomic bombing of the Japanese city in 1945. The ceremony in Nagasaki remembers those who were killed and those who survived, and renews the city's call for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.history: On the morning of 9 August 1945 a United States aircraft dropped an atomic bomb over the Urakami district of Nagasaki at 11:02; the intended target, Kokura, had been obscured by cloud. Estimates of the number who died by the end of that year range from about 60,000 to 80,000, and many more suffered lasting effects. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. The ground around the hypocentre was laid out as a memorial park, where the Peace Statue by Seibo Kitamura was completed in 1955, and the city holds its peace memorial ceremony there each 9 August.
memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.traditions: The ceremony takes place in Peace Park, attended by the mayor, survivors, bereaved families and representatives of many countries. A silence is observed at 11:02, the time of the blast, and a bell is rung. The mayor reads the Peace Declaration, calling for nuclear disarmament, and water is offered in memory of those who died of thirst. In the evening lanterns are floated and candles are lit at the hypocentre.
funFacts: The silence in Nagasaki is observed at 11:02, the moment of the explosion on 9 August 1945.
The ten-metre Peace Statue by Seibo Kitamura raises one hand towards the sky and stretches the other out for peace.
Nagasaki's Fountain of Peace, opened in 1969, remembers those who died searching for water.

memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.intro: South Korea observes 18 May as the memorial day of the Gwangju Democratic Uprising. It remembers the citizens of Gwangju and South Jeolla Province who died in 1980 while demanding an end to military rule and the lifting of martial law.
memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.history: In May 1980 the military government extended martial law across South Korea and closed the universities. Student protests in Gwangju that began on 18 May were met with force by paratroopers, residents joined the demonstrations, and for several days the city was held by its own citizens before troops retook it on 27 May. Estimates of the number killed vary considerably. The uprising was officially reassessed in the following decades, and 18 May was designated a national memorial day in 1997.
memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.traditions: The government ceremony is held each 18 May in Gwangju, at the May 18th National Cemetery or at the Democracy Square in front of the former provincial office building, often with the president in attendance. Bereaved families, participants in the uprising, officials and students take part, and the programme includes a commemorative address, memorial performances and the collective singing of March for the Beloved. Wreaths are laid at the cemetery throughout the day.
funFacts: Archives documenting the uprising were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2011.
March for the Beloved is sung at the ceremony and is the movement's best-known song.
Victims were first buried at Mangwol-dong; the May 18th National Cemetery was later built nearby.

memorial_kr_memorial_day.intro: Memorial Day (Hyeonchungil) on 6 June honours the soldiers and civilians who died for South Korea, especially in the Korean War of 1950 to 1953.
memorial_kr_memorial_day.history: The day was established in 1956, three years after the armistice, to remember the fallen of the war. The date follows the traditional calendar, on which early June marks the start of the season for tending ancestral graves.
memorial_kr_memorial_day.traditions: At 10 a.m. a siren sounds nationwide for one minute of silence. The president leads a ceremony at the Seoul National Cemetery, where families lay flowers on the graves, and flags are flown at half mast throughout the country.
funFacts: The Korean War has never formally ended; only an armistice was signed in 1953.
The Seoul National Cemetery in Dongjak-gu is the resting place of more than 160,000 people.
Because it is a day of mourning, the national flag is raised to half mast rather than full height.

memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.intro: Freedom Defenders' Day, Laisves gyneju diena, is marked in Lithuania on 13 January. It honours the unarmed civilians killed when Soviet forces moved against the television tower and broadcasting centre in Vilnius in 1991, as the country defended its restored independence.
memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.history: Lithuania declared the restoration of its independence in March 1990. During the night of 12 to 13 January 1991 Soviet troops and armoured vehicles moved on the Vilnius television tower and the radio and television building, where crowds had gathered unarmed to protect them. Fourteen people were killed and more than a hundred were injured. Crowds went on guarding the parliament building for weeks afterwards. Lithuania later made 13 January a state day of commemoration, and the Seimas awards an annual Freedom Prize on the anniversary.
memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.traditions: Households across Lithuania light candles in their windows on the morning of the anniversary, and the national flag is flown with a black ribbon attached. Bonfires burn at the television tower and outside the Seimas, which holds a ceremonial sitting and presents the Freedom Prize. Flowers are laid at the victims' graves at Antakalnis Cemetery in Vilnius, and forget-me-not pins are worn as a sign of remembrance.
funFacts: The forget-me-not flower has become the emblem of remembrance for the events of January 1991.
The national flag is flown with a black mourning ribbon attached on Freedom Defenders' Day.
The victims of the January events are buried at Antakalnis Cemetery in Vilnius, where ceremonies are held each year.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.intro: 20 January remembers the defenders of the barricades of January 1991, when people in Riga protected the young Latvian democracy against Soviet special forces.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.history: After the Soviet crackdown in Vilnius on 13 January 1991, tens of thousands of Latvians built barricades around the parliament, the television centre and the bridges of Riga. On 20 January the OMON special police stormed the Interior Ministry; five people were killed, among them two cameramen filming the events.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.traditions: Bonfires are lit on Dome Square in Old Riga as they were in 1991, and wreaths are laid at the memorial stones in Bastejkalns park where the victims fell. The Barricades Museum in Old Riga keeps the memory alive with original film footage.
funFacts: The barricades were built from trucks, tractors and concrete blocks brought in from all over Latvia.
Farmers kept the defenders supplied with hot food and firewood for days.
The Barricades Museum was opened in 2001 in a house on Krāmu iela in Old Riga.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.intro: 4 July commemorates the genocide against the Jews of Latvia during the German occupation, in which around 70,000 Latvian Jews were murdered.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.history: On 4 July 1941 the Great Choral Synagogue in Riga was set on fire with people inside, as were other synagogues in the city. Mass shootings followed, above all at Rumbula and Biķernieki in late 1941. The remembrance day was established in 1990.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the ruins of the Great Choral Synagogue on Gogoļa iela and at the Rumbula and Biķernieki memorials. The Žanis Lipke Memorial honours Latvians who hid Jews at the risk of their own lives.
funFacts: Žanis Lipke, a Riga dock worker, saved more than 50 Jews and is honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.
The memorial at the synagogue ruins includes a wall of names of the rescuers.
Before the war about 93,000 Jews lived in Latvia, roughly five percent of the population.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.intro: 14 June remembers the victims of communist terror, in particular the mass deportation of 14 June 1941, when more than 15,000 people were taken from Latvia to Siberia in a single night.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.history: On the night of 13 to 14 June 1941 the Soviet authorities arrested families across Latvia, separated men from women and children and sent them east in freight wagons. Many did not survive the first winter. A second, even larger deportation followed on 25 March 1949, which is also a day of remembrance.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.traditions: Flags fly with black ribbons, and wreaths are laid at Torņakalns railway station in Riga, from where the trains left. Names of the deported are read aloud, and the Museum of the Occupation holds a memorial event.
funFacts: A memorial wagon at Torņakalns station shows the conditions of the deportations.
Together the deportations of 1941 and 1949 affected almost 60,000 people in Latvia.
In 1987 a flower-laying at the Freedom Monument on 14 June became one of the first public protests of the Latvian independence movement.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.intro: On the first Sunday of December Latvia remembers the Latvians killed during the Soviet 'Latvian Operation' of 1937 and 1938 and all victims of the communist regime.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.history: On 3 December 1937 the Soviet secret police NKVD began the 'Latvian Operation', in which more than 22,000 Latvians living in the Soviet Union were arrested and some 16,000 shot. The remembrance day recalls this and the later repressions after 1940.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.traditions: Memorial services are held at the Freedom Monument in Riga and in churches, and candles are lit at memorials. The Museum of the Occupation and historians present research on the fate of the victims.
funFacts: The Latvian Operation was one of several 'national operations' of the Great Terror.
Many of the victims were descendants of Latvian farmers who had settled in Russia in the 19th century.
The memorial site at Levashovo near St Petersburg holds a monument to the Latvian victims.

memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.intro: 23 August is the European Day of Remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism, the anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 and of the Baltic Way of 1989.
memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.history: On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe, which sealed the fate of the Baltic states. Fifty years later, on 23 August 1989, about two million people formed a human chain from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius to demand independence.
memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Freedom Monument in Riga, and candles are lit in memory of the victims of both regimes. The Baltic Way is recalled with exhibitions and films, and the day is marked across the European Union.
funFacts: The Baltic Way stretched about 675 kilometres across the three countries.
The documents of the Baltic Way were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2009.
In 2008 the European Parliament called for 23 August to become a day of remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism.

memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.intro: Heroes' Commemoration Day on 22 June recalls the Battle of Cēsis in 1919, a turning point of the Latvian War of Independence.
memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.history: Between 19 and 23 June 1919 Estonian troops and Latvian units defeated the German Baltic Landeswehr near Cēsis. The victory ended German plans to control the Baltic and secured the government of Kārlis Ulmanis. Estonia celebrates the same battle on 23 June as Victory Day.
memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the monument to the fallen in Cēsis and at the Brothers' Cemetery in Riga. Latvian and Estonian officials often commemorate the battle together.
funFacts: Latvian schoolboys from Cēsis fought in the battle as a volunteer company.
Cēsis Castle, one of the best-preserved medieval castles in Latvia, overlooks the town.
The battle is sometimes called the 'Battle of Võnnu' in Estonia, after the Estonian name of Cēsis.

memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.intro: 11 August honours the freedom fighters of the Latvian War of Independence and marks the peace treaty with Soviet Russia of 1920 that ended the war.
memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.history: In the Treaty of Riga of 11 August 1920 Soviet Russia recognised Latvia's independence 'for all time'. The war of 1918 to 1920 had been fought against Bolshevik forces, German units and the West Russian Volunteer Army. About 3,000 Latvian soldiers died.
memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the Freedom Monument and at the Brothers' Cemetery in Riga, where the fallen of the war are buried. The National Armed Forces hold a ceremony, and veterans' organisations remember the volunteers.
funFacts: The Brothers' Cemetery in Riga was designed by sculptor Kārlis Zāle, who also created the Freedom Monument.
The Freedom Monument, unveiled in 1935, bears the inscription 'For Fatherland and Freedom'.
The Soviet Union broke the 'eternal' peace treaty twenty years later with the occupation of 1940.

memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.intro: 2 March remembers the Latvian national partisans, the 'Forest Brothers', who fought against the Soviet occupation after 1944.
memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.history: The date recalls the Battle of Stompaki on 2 and 3 March 1945 in Latgale, the largest engagement between Latvian partisans and Soviet forces. Around 20,000 Latvians took part in the armed resistance, which lasted into the 1950s. The remembrance day was added to the law in 2020.
memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.traditions: Wreaths are laid at partisan memorials and bunkers in the forests, and the National Armed Forces hold ceremonies. Local museums and historians tell the stories of individual resistance groups.
funFacts: At Stompaki about 350 partisans held out against several thousand Soviet troops before breaking out of the encirclement.
The last known Latvian partisan came out of hiding only in the 1990s.
Similar days of remembrance exist in Estonia and Lithuania.

memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.intro: 17 March honours the national resistance movement, above all the Latvian Central Council, which demanded the restoration of independence during the German occupation in 1944.
memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.history: On 17 March 1944, 188 leading Latvian politicians and public figures signed a memorandum calling for the restoration of the independent Republic of Latvia. The Central Council was led by Konstantīns Čakste, who was arrested by the Gestapo and died in a concentration camp in 1945.
memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the memorial plaque to the Central Council in Riga, and the president or speaker of parliament gives a commemorative address. Historians recall the many forms of resistance to both occupying powers.
funFacts: Konstantīns Čakste was the son of Latvia's first president, Jānis Čakste.
The Central Council also organised boat crossings that helped refugees escape to Sweden.
The memorandum was smuggled out of the country and handed to the Western Allies.

memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.intro: 21 November remembers the 54 people who died when the roof of a supermarket collapsed in the Zolitūde district of Riga in 2013.
memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.history: On the evening of 21 November 2013 the roof of a Maxima supermarket collapsed during shopping hours; among the dead were three firefighters killed when a second section fell during the rescue. It was the deadliest disaster in Latvia since independence and led to stricter building rules.
memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.traditions: A memorial service is held at the memorial in Zolitūde, and candles are lit at the site. Flags fly at half mast, and the names of the victims are read aloud.
funFacts: The prime minister resigned six days after the disaster, taking political responsibility.
The memorial at the site bears the names of all 54 victims.
Latvia declared three days of national mourning after the disaster, from 23 to 25 November 2013.

memorial_mg_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day in Madagascar is observed on 29 March. It remembers those who died in the Malagasy uprising against French colonial rule, which began on that date in 1947, and in the repression that followed it.
memorial_mg_martyrs_day.history: On the evening of 29 March 1947 Malagasy nationalists launched coordinated attacks on military posts and French-owned plantations in the east of the island, around Moramanga and Manakara. The rising spread across a large part of Madagascar and was put down by French forces over nearly two years, ending in 1949; estimates of the number of dead vary widely between sources. In 1967 the Malagasy government declared 29 March a day of mourning, and official commemorations have been held annually since then.
memorial_mg_martyrs_day.traditions: The day is a public holiday observed as a day of mourning. The president and other officials lay wreaths at monuments to the dead, and a central ceremony is held at Moramanga, where the uprising began. Churches hold services, schools and broadcasters revisit the events of 1947, and the museum dedicated to the uprising in Moramanga receives visitors throughout the day.
funFacts: The uprising began on the evening of 29 March 1947 in the east of the island.
A national museum devoted to the uprising was inaugurated in Moramanga in 2012.
Madagascar became independent from France on 26 June 1960.

memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.intro: Genocide Remembrance Day on 28 May commemorates the Ovaherero and Nama who were killed under German colonial rule between 1904 and 1908.
memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.history: After the uprising of 1904 the German colonial army drove the Herero into the Omaheke desert and imprisoned survivors in camps such as Shark Island. Tens of thousands died. Germany officially recognised the events as genocide in 2021. Namibia observed the day for the first time in 2025, choosing the date on which the camps were ordered closed in 1907.
memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.traditions: A national ceremony with a minute of silence and candle lighting is held, and descendants of the victims hold memorial gatherings in Okahandja, Swakopmund and Lüderitz. The day is a public holiday.
funFacts: The genocide of the Herero and Nama is considered the first genocide of the 20th century.
In 2018 Germany returned human remains that had been taken to Berlin for racial research.
The Genocide Memorial in Windhoek was unveiled in 2014 on the site of the former equestrian monument to German colonial soldiers.

memorial_na_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day is a public holiday in Namibia, observed on 26 August. It honours those who died in the struggle for Namibian independence and marks the first armed clash of the liberation war, which took place at Omugulugwombashe in 1966.
memorial_na_heroes_day.history: In 1966 the United Nations General Assembly ended South Africa's mandate over South West Africa, but South African rule continued. SWAPO had formed its armed wing, the People's Liberation Army of Namibia, in 1962 and established a camp at Omugulugwombashe in the north. On 26 August 1966 South African forces attacked the camp in the first battle of the Namibian War of Independence. The war lasted until the end of the 1980s, and Namibia became independent in 1990. The anniversary is now a national holiday and is known internationally as Namibia Day.
memorial_na_heroes_day.traditions: The main ceremony is held at Heroes' Acre, the national memorial south of Windhoek, where the president lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and addresses the nation. Military parades, the laying of flowers and the awarding of medals to veterans form part of the programme. Commemorations are also held in the north and at regional memorials, with church services and readings of the names of the fallen.
funFacts: Heroes' Acre, the national memorial outside Windhoek, was inaugurated on Heroes' Day in 2002.
The United Nations marks 26 August as Namibia Day.
The first battle of the independence war took place at Omugulugwombashe on 26 August 1966.

memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.intro: Dodenherdenking, the Remembrance of the Dead, is held in the Netherlands every 4 May. It remembers all Dutch civilians and members of the armed forces who have died in wars and peacekeeping missions since the outbreak of the Second World War, and precedes Liberation Day on 5 May.
memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.history: The Netherlands was occupied by Germany from 1940 until the surrender of German forces in the country in May 1945. Commemorations of the war dead began in the first years after the liberation and were given a fixed national form on 4 May, the eve of Liberation Day. At first only Dutch victims of the Second World War were remembered; since 1961 the commemoration has also included those who died in later conflicts and in peacekeeping operations, among them the Indonesian war, Lebanon and Bosnia.
memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.traditions: Flags fly at half-mast from six in the evening. At eight o'clock the whole country observes two minutes of silence: trains and traffic stop, broadcasts fall quiet and people stand still in the street. The central ceremony is at the National Monument on Dam Square in Amsterdam, where the king and queen lay a wreath, and it is broadcast live. Afterwards the flags are raised again while the national anthem is played, and flowers are laid at local monuments.
funFacts: The two minutes of silence begin at eight in the evening, and public transport across the country comes to a halt.
Flags fly at half-mast from six in the evening until the silence ends, then are raised while the anthem plays.
Liberation Day follows on 5 May, marking the German surrender in the Netherlands in 1945.

memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.intro: In Norway, 22 July is a day of remembrance for the victims of the attacks of 2011, when a bomb was detonated in the government quarter in Oslo and a shooting took place at a Labour youth camp on the island of Utøya.
memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.history: On 22 July 2011 a car bomb exploded outside government buildings in central Oslo, killing eight people. The attacker then travelled to Utøya, where the Workers' Youth League was holding its summer camp, and killed sixty-nine more, most of them teenagers. Seventy-seven people died in all, making it the deadliest attack in Norway since the Second World War. The perpetrator was convicted and sentenced to preventive detention. The anniversary has been marked nationally every year since, with a large commemoration on the round anniversaries.
memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.traditions: Flags fly at half-mast. Members of the royal family, the prime minister, survivors and bereaved families attend a ceremony in the government quarter where the names of the dead are read aloud, followed by a memorial service in Oslo Cathedral and the ringing of church bells there and across the country. Flowers are laid at the Iron Roses memorial beside the cathedral and at the memorial site by Utøya.
funFacts: Seventy-seven people were killed, sixty-nine of them at the youth camp on Utøya.
The Iron Roses memorial by Oslo Cathedral holds a thousand hand-forged roses and dates from 2019.
The 22 July Centre in Oslo documents the attacks and is widely used for school visits.

memorial_pa_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day, Día de los Mártires, is a day of national mourning in Panama observed on 9 January. It remembers the Panamanians killed in January 1964 during clashes in the United States-controlled Panama Canal Zone over the right to fly the Panamanian flag there.
memorial_pa_martyrs_day.history: From 1903 the United States controlled the Canal Zone, a strip dividing Panama in two. An earlier agreement provided for both flags to fly together at civilian sites in the zone, but at Balboa High School only the American flag was raised. On 9 January 1964 students from the Instituto Nacional went to the school with a Panamanian flag; it was torn in the confrontation that followed, and unrest spread across the zone for several days. More than twenty Panamanians and several United States soldiers died. The events helped lead to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, under which the canal passed to Panama at the end of 1999.
memorial_pa_martyrs_day.traditions: Public offices close and flags fly at half-mast. Officials, veterans' associations and student delegations lay wreaths at memorials in Panama City, above all at the former Balboa High School, now the Ascanio Arosemena Training Center, where the names of the dead are inscribed. The names are read aloud at commemorative acts, and schools hold assemblies on the history of the canal and Panamanian sovereignty.
funFacts: Ascanio Arosemena, a student killed on 9 January 1964, is remembered as the first of the martyrs.
The former Balboa High School now houses a Panama Canal training centre named after him.
Panama took full control of the canal on 31 December 1999, under treaties signed in 1977.

memorial_pg_remembrance_day.intro: Remembrance Day on 23 July honours Papua New Guineans who served and died in the Second World War, especially the soldiers of the Papuan Infantry Battalion.
memorial_pg_remembrance_day.history: On 23 July 1942 the Papuan Infantry Battalion fought its first engagement against Japanese troops near Awala at the start of the Kokoda campaign. The day became a national holiday after independence in 1975.
memorial_pg_remembrance_day.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the Bomana War Cemetery near Port Moresby and at the Remembrance Park in the capital. Veterans' families, the defence force and schoolchildren take part, and the Last Post is sounded.
funFacts: Papua New Guineans who carried wounded soldiers along the Kokoda Track became known as the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels'.
Bomana War Cemetery is the largest war cemetery in the Pacific with more than 3,800 graves.
The Papuan Infantry Battalion was the first indigenous military unit of the country.

memorial_ph_day_of_valor.intro: Araw ng Kagitingan, the Day of Valor, is a national holiday in the Philippines observed on 9 April. It honours the Filipino and American soldiers who defended Bataan and Corregidor in 1942 and those who died in captivity afterwards.
memorial_ph_day_of_valor.history: On 9 April 1942 the defenders of the Bataan Peninsula surrendered to Japanese forces after months of fighting, and tens of thousands of Filipino and American troops were forced on the march to Camp O'Donnell, during which many died. Corregidor fell the following month. President Carlos P. Garcia signed Republic Act No. 3022 in 1961, making 9 April a national observance then known as Bataan Day. It was later renamed Araw ng Kagitingan, the Day of Valor. Between 1980 and 1987 the date was temporarily moved to 6 May before returning to 9 April.
memorial_ph_day_of_valor.traditions: The main national rite is held at the Mount Samat National Shrine, the Dambana ng Kagitingan, in Pilar, Bataan, where the President or a representative lays a wreath at the memorial cross. Surviving veterans, their families and diplomats from the United States and Japan usually attend, and the programme includes prayers, honours for the war dead and addresses. The day falls within Philippine Veterans Week, from 5 to 11 April.
funFacts: Dambana ng Kagitingan, the Shrine of Valor, stands on Mount Samat above the peninsula where the 1942 fighting took place.
The observance was created in 1961 as Bataan Day under Republic Act No. 3022 and later renamed Araw ng Kagitingan.
From 1980 to 1987 the day was held on 6 May before it was returned to its original date of 9 April.

memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.intro: National Heroes Day is a public holiday in the Philippines, observed on the last Monday of August. It honours the Filipinos who fought and died for the country's freedom, from the revolutionaries of 1896 to soldiers, resistance fighters and later generations.
memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.history: The date recalls the start of the Philippine Revolution against Spanish rule in late August 1896, when members of the Katipunan led by Andrés Bonifacio tore up their tax certificates in an act remembered as the Cry of Pugad Lawin, also known as the Cry of Balintawak. Because the exact day and place remained disputed, lawmakers fixed the observance to the final week of August. Act No. 3827 of 1931 first set it on the last Sunday of August, and Republic Act No. 9492 moved it to the last Monday in 2007.
memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.traditions: The president usually leads a wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig, attended by an honour guard and government officials. Local governments hold their own rites at monuments and plazas, and flags are displayed at public buildings. Commemorative speeches often widen the meaning of heroism to include ordinary Filipinos such as overseas workers and health workers.
funFacts: The law names no specific heroes, leaving the day open to honour both famous figures and unnamed ones.
Act No. 3827 first established the observance in 1931, on the last Sunday of August.
Since 2007 the holiday falls on the last Monday of August, so its date shifts each year.

memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.intro: The Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Katyn Massacre is observed in Poland on 13 April. It honours the Polish officers, police officers and civilians murdered by the Soviet secret police in the spring of 1940.
memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.history: In the spring of 1940, following a decision of the Soviet Politburo, the NKVD shot thousands of Polish prisoners of war and detainees at Katyn and other sites, among them army officers, police, border guards, teachers, doctors and lawyers. On 13 April 1943 German radio announced the discovery of mass graves in the Katyn forest. The Soviet Union denied responsibility for decades and admitted it only on 13 April 1990. The Polish Sejm established the national day of remembrance by resolution in November 2007.
memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.traditions: State ceremonies are held at the Katyn Museum in Warsaw and at the Polish war cemeteries at Katyn, Kharkiv and Mednoye, with wreaths, candles and a roll call of the dead. Flags are flown at half-mast with mourning ribbons and Masses are said in churches across the country. Families of the victims, officials and soldiers take part, and oak trees planted in memory of individual victims are tended in many towns.
funFacts: The graves in the Katyn forest were announced on 13 April 1943; the Soviet Union admitted responsibility on the same date in 1990.
The Polish Sejm established the national day of remembrance by resolution in November 2007.
Polish war cemeteries for the victims were opened at Katyn, Kharkiv and Mednoye.

memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.intro: Every 19 April Poland remembers the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which began on that date in 1943. The day honours the Jewish fighters who took up arms against the German forces sent to liquidate the ghetto, and the hundreds of thousands of people murdered there and in the death camps.
memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.history: Warsaw's Jewish population was confined to a sealed ghetto in 1940. During the summer of 1942 the great majority of its inhabitants were deported to the Treblinka extermination camp. When German units returned on 19 April 1943 to complete the liquidation, the Jewish Combat Organisation under Mordechai Anielewicz and the Jewish Military Union resisted with a small stock of weapons. Fighting and the systematic burning of the district lasted until 16 May 1943. The anniversary has been marked in Warsaw since the first years after the war.
memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.traditions: At noon sirens sound across Warsaw for one minute. Officials, survivors and their families lay flowers at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes in Muranów and at the Umschlagplatz memorial, and walk the Path of Remembrance through the former ghetto. The POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews hands out paper daffodils, which people pin to their clothes; the flower recalls the yellow bouquets that the last surviving commander, Marek Edelman, laid at the monument each year.
funFacts: The daffodil became the symbol of the day because Marek Edelman, the last surviving commander, laid yellow flowers at the monument each year.
Sirens sound across Warsaw for one minute at noon on 19 April.
The Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, by Nathan Rapoport, was unveiled in 1948 among the ruins of the district.

memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.intro: The National Day of Remembrance of the Warsaw Uprising is marked in Poland on 1 August. It honours the insurgents and the civilians of Warsaw who died during the rising against the German occupation in 1944.
memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.history: The Warsaw Uprising began at 17:00 on 1 August 1944, the moment known as hour W, when units of the Polish Home Army under General Tadeusz Bór-Komorowski attacked German positions across the city. Colonel Antoni Chruściel commanded the forces inside Warsaw. The fighting lasted 63 days before the Home Army capitulated on 2 October; thousands of insurgents and far more civilians were killed, and much of the city was destroyed afterwards. Poland established 1 August as an official day of remembrance by law in 2009.
memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.traditions: At 17:00 on 1 August sirens sound across Warsaw and much of Poland. Traffic stops, pedestrians stand still and many drivers step out of their cars for a minute. Wreaths are laid at the Powązki Military Cemetery and at the monuments to the uprising, veterans attend the official ceremonies, and the Warsaw Uprising Museum opens without charge. In the evening people gather in the streets to sing wartime songs.
funFacts: The starting moment is called hour W, after the Polish word wybuch, meaning outbreak.
The fighting lasted 63 days, far longer than its planners had expected.
The Warsaw Uprising Museum opened in 2004, on the sixtieth anniversary of the rising.

memorial_py_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day, Dia de los Heroes, is a national holiday in Paraguay on 1 March. It honours Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez and all Paraguayans who died in the country's wars, above all the Paraguayan War of 1864 to 1870.
memorial_py_heroes_day.history: The date recalls the Battle of Cerro Cora on 1 March 1870, the last engagement of the Paraguayan War, in which President Francisco Solano Lopez was killed after refusing to surrender. The war against the allied forces of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay had lasted more than five years and left Paraguay devastated. Lopez was later reinterpreted in Paraguay as a national hero rather than a defeated leader, and 1 March was set aside to honour the country's war dead, with commemorative activities continuing through the month.
memorial_py_heroes_day.traditions: The central ceremony takes place at the Panteon Nacional de los Heroes in Asuncion, where the remains of Solano Lopez and other national figures rest. The President and members of the government lay wreaths, an honour guard stands watch and military honours are rendered. Wreaths are also laid at Cerro Cora National Park in Amambay, the site of the 1870 battle, and at monuments in towns across the country.
funFacts: The Battle of Cerro Cora on 1 March 1870 ended the Paraguayan War, one of the deadliest conflicts in South American history.
The Panteon Nacional de los Heroes in Asuncion holds the remains of Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez.
Cerro Cora, in the Amambay department, is preserved as a national park and place of remembrance.

memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.intro: Kwibuka, meaning remember in Kinyarwanda, is Rwanda's day of remembrance for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. It is observed on 7 April and opens a national mourning period that lasts about a hundred days.
memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.history: The genocide began in April 1994, after the aircraft carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down on 6 April, and continued for roughly a hundred days until the Rwandan Patriotic Front took control of the country in July. Those killed were overwhelmingly Tutsi, along with Hutu who opposed the killings; estimates of the death toll differ between sources. Rwanda has commemorated 7 April since the years immediately after the genocide, and the United Nations designated the date an international day of reflection, first observed in 2004.
memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.traditions: The president lights a flame of remembrance at the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Gisozi and addresses the nation, followed by a national ceremony and a night vigil. The week after 7 April is an official week of mourning, with flags at half-mast, subdued broadcasting and music, and gatherings at memorial sites across the country. Walks of remembrance are held, and the mourning period continues until Liberation Day on 4 July.
funFacts: Kwibuka means remember in Kinyarwanda and gives the annual commemoration its name.
The mourning period runs from 7 April to Liberation Day on 4 July, about a hundred days.
The Kigali Genocide Memorial at Gisozi was inaugurated in April 2004, ten years after the genocide.

memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.intro: The Day of Uprising Against Occupation is a Slovenian state holiday marked each year on 27 April. It remembers the founding of the resistance movement that opposed the occupation and partition of Slovene territory during the Second World War.
memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.history: In April 1941 Slovene territory was occupied and partitioned by Germany, Italy and Hungary. On 26 April 1941, at the Ljubljana home of the critic Josip Vidmar, representatives of the Communist Party of Slovenia, Christian socialists, the Sokol movement and cultural figures founded the Anti-Imperialist Front, which was renamed the Liberation Front of the Slovene Nation later that year. For about two decades it was believed that the meeting had taken place on 27 April, and that date became the Day of the Liberation Front. It was kept, and the holiday renamed, after Slovenia became independent in 1991.
memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.traditions: The day is a work-free state holiday. The central state ceremony is held on the eve of the holiday, each year in a different town connected with the resistance. Across the country there are wreath-layings at partisan monuments, commemorative marches and local gatherings, while veterans' organisations, museums and schools host exhibitions and talks about the occupation years.
funFacts: The holiday falls on 27 April, although historians date the founding meeting to 26 April 1941.
Until 1991 the day was known as Day of the Liberation Front, dan Osvobodilne fronte.
The movement began under the name Anti-Imperialist Front and took its later name in 1941.

memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.intro: The Slovak National Uprising Anniversary is a public holiday in Slovakia on 29 August. It marks the day in 1944 when Slovak soldiers and partisans rose in arms against Nazi German occupation and the collaborationist wartime Slovak regime.
memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.history: The uprising began on 29 August 1944 and was directed by the Slovak National Council, which brought together communist and non-communist resistance groups. Lieutenant Colonel Jan Golian led the insurgent forces at first, and Division General Rudolf Viest took command on 7 October. The insurgents briefly controlled a large part of Slovak territory before German units pushed them back and took Banska Bystrica on 27 October 1944. Fighters then continued in the mountains as partisans until the country was liberated in spring 1945. The anniversary is today a national holiday.
memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.traditions: Official ceremonies centre on Banska Bystrica, the insurgent capital of 1944, where the Museum of the Slovak National Uprising and its monument stand. State representatives lay wreaths, military honours are rendered and veterans' associations take part. Wreath-layings, exhibitions and commemorative marches are also held at partisan memorials and village monuments across Slovakia, and public buildings display the national flag.
funFacts: The uprising lasted about two months, from 29 August 1944 to the fall of Banska Bystrica on 27 October 1944.
The Museum of the Slovak National Uprising was founded in 1955; its distinctive split building in Banska Bystrica was completed in 1969.
After the uprising was suppressed, its fighters kept up resistance in the mountains until liberation in April 1945.

memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.intro: 17 November commemorates the students' protests of 1939 and 1989 and the beginning of the Velvet Revolution that ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.history: On 17 November 1939 the Nazi occupiers closed Czech universities and executed nine student leaders. On 17 November 1989 a student demonstration in Prague was violently dispersed, triggering the mass protests of the Velvet Revolution. In Slovakia the anniversary remains a state holiday, but is not a day off work.
memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.traditions: Gatherings with candles and speeches are held in Bratislava and other towns, and people ring keys as they did in 1989. Concerts and discussions with participants of the revolution take place, and the day is also International Students' Day.
funFacts: Jingling keys became the sound of the Velvet Revolution, symbolising the message 'time to go' to the communists.
In Bratislava the first large demonstration took place on the Square of the Slovak National Uprising.
Alexander Dubček, the face of the 1968 Prague Spring, returned to public life during the revolution.

memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.intro: On 2 November, All Souls' Day, San Marino commemorates all those who died in war, together with the Catholic remembrance of the dead.
memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.history: The tiny republic remained neutral in both world wars but was bombed by mistake by British aircraft in June 1944, killing 63 people, and took in about 100,000 refugees. The commemoration on All Souls' Day is one of the country's official holidays.
memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.traditions: Families visit the cemeteries, above all Montalbo cemetery, and lay flowers and light candles on the graves. A ceremony honours the war dead of the republic, and the Captains Regent take part in a memorial mass.
funFacts: San Marino's population is only about 34,000, so almost every family had relatives among the wartime refugees.
A plaque at the railway station remembers the victims of the 1944 bombing.
All Souls' Day has been observed by the Catholic Church since the 11th century.

memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.intro: Atatürk Memorial Day is observed throughout Turkey on 10 November, the anniversary of the death of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1938. The founder and first president of the Turkish Republic is remembered at the exact hour of his death with a silence kept across the whole country.
memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.history: Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish national movement after the First World War and became the first president of the republic proclaimed in 1923, carrying through far-reaching reforms of the state, the law, the alphabet and education. His health declined through 1938, and he died of cirrhosis of the liver at 09:05 on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul. A state funeral was held in Ankara on 21 November, with delegations from seventeen countries. His remains were moved to the Anıtkabir mausoleum in Ankara on the anniversary of his death in 1953.
memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.traditions: At 09:05 sirens sound across the country and everything stops: people rise from their desks, traffic halts and drivers step out of their cars for the silence, which is followed by the national anthem. Flags fly at half-mast, and the president, ministers and military commanders lay a wreath at Anıtkabir, where large crowds file past through the day. Schools hold memorial assemblies with speeches, poems and readings.
funFacts: The silence begins at 09:05, the exact time of Atatürk's death on 10 November 1938.
He was laid to rest at Anıtkabir in Ankara in 1953, after fifteen years in the city's Ethnography Museum.
At Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, where he died, the clock in his room is kept at 09:05.

memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.intro: Ukraine marks 26 April as the day of remembrance for the Chernobyl disaster. It honours those who died in the 1986 accident at the nuclear power plant, the emergency workers who contained its aftermath and the residents who lost their homes.
memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.history: At 01:23 on 26 April 1986 reactor number four of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, near the city of Pripyat in what was then the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, was destroyed during a test. Firefighters and plant staff were exposed to severe radiation, and Pripyat was evacuated the following day, its residents leaving with few belongings. Hundreds of thousands of workers, later known as liquidators, took part in the clean-up. In 2016 the United Nations designated 26 April as an international remembrance day.
memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.traditions: Commemorations begin at night. In Slavutych, the town built for the displaced plant workers, people gather in the central square shortly after midnight, place candles and flowers before the memorial, and a bell is rung at the hour of the accident. Church services are held in Chernobyl and Kyiv, wreaths are laid at monuments to the firefighters and liquidators, and flags fly at half-mast.
funFacts: The reactor was destroyed at 01:23 at night, the hour at which memorial bells are rung.
Pripyat was evacuated on 27 April 1986, the day after the accident, and has stood empty since.
The United Nations designated 26 April International Chernobyl Disaster Remembrance Day in 2016.

memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.intro: Holodomor Remembrance Day is observed in Ukraine on the fourth Saturday of November. It remembers the victims of the famine of 1932 and 1933, when millions of Ukrainians starved to death under Soviet rule, and of the other famines of the Soviet period.
memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.history: Grain requisitions and the forced collectivisation of agriculture stripped Ukrainian villages of food through the winter of 1932 and the spring of 1933, while people were prevented from leaving to look for it. Millions died; the exact number remains disputed. For decades the famine could not be spoken of publicly. President Leonid Kuchma created a national day of remembrance by decree in 1998. Its name was widened in 2000 and 2004 to include the famines of 1921 to 1923 and 1946 to 1947, and narrowed again in 2007 to focus on the Holodomor.
memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.traditions: At four in the afternoon the country observes a minute of silence, and people light a candle and set it in the window at home. Flags fly at half-mast and entertainment programmes are suspended. Ceremonies are held at the National Museum of the Holodomor-Genocide in Kyiv, where officials lay ears of wheat and symbolic vessels of grain, memorial services take place in churches, and candles are placed at monuments in villages across the country.
funFacts: Candles are lit at four in the afternoon and placed in windows across Ukraine.
The day falls on the fourth Saturday of November, so its date changes each year.
Canada has observed a Ukrainian Famine and Genocide Memorial Day on the same date since 2008.

memorial_ug_martyrs_day.intro: Uganda Martyrs Day is a public holiday in Uganda on 3 June. It remembers the Catholic and Anglican converts put to death in the kingdom of Buganda in the 1880s, among them Charles Lwanga and his companions, who died on that date in 1886.
memorial_ug_martyrs_day.history: Between 1885 and 1887 a group of Christian converts at the court of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda were executed for refusing to renounce their faith. Twenty-two were Catholic and twenty-three Anglican. The largest group, including Charles Lwanga, died on 3 June 1886 at Namugongo. The Catholic martyrs were beatified in 1920 and canonised by Pope Paul VI at St Peter's Basilica in Rome on 18 October 1964, and 3 June entered the General Roman Calendar as their feast day.
memorial_ug_martyrs_day.traditions: Pilgrims travel to the shrines at Namugongo outside Kampala, where a Catholic basilica built in 1968 and an Anglican memorial site stand close together. Many walk for days from across Uganda and from neighbouring countries to reach them. Open-air Masses and Anglican services are held on the day, and the Munyonyo Martyrs' Shrine near Kampala also draws visitors. Both churches mark the anniversary on the same date.
funFacts: The Catholic martyrs were beatified in 1920 and canonised on 18 October 1964 by Pope Paul VI in Rome.
The Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo was built in 1968 and has drawn large pilgrimages since the 1980s.
The Munyonyo Martyrs' Shrine was raised as a thanksgiving monument for the canonisation of the martyrs.

memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.intro: The International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade is observed worldwide on 25 March. Established by the United Nations, it honours the millions of African men, women and children who were enslaved and shipped across the Atlantic over some four centuries.
memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.history: The transatlantic slave trade carried captive Africans to the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century, and the United Nations describes it as one of the gravest violations of human rights in history. The General Assembly designated 25 March as an annual day of remembrance in 2007, the year in which two hundred years had passed since Britain abolished its slave trade. The day was first observed in 2008 under the theme 'Breaking the Silence, Lest We Forget', and each year since has been given its own theme.
memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.traditions: The General Assembly holds a commemorative meeting at United Nations Headquarters in New York, with descendants of the enslaved, scholars, artists and diplomats taking part. Flowers and wreaths are laid at the Ark of Return, the permanent memorial in the visitors' plaza. Member states, schools, museums and UNESCO mark the day with lectures, exhibitions, concerts and readings on the history of slavery and its consequences today.
funFacts: The Ark of Return, the permanent memorial at United Nations Headquarters, was unveiled in 2015.
It was designed by the Haitian-American architect Rodney Leon, who also designed New York's African Burial Ground memorial.
The first observance in 2008 carried the theme 'Breaking the Silence, Lest We Forget'.

memorial_us_memorial_day.intro: Memorial Day on the last Monday in May is the U.S. day of remembrance for fallen American soldiers. It is also the unofficial start of summer in the U.S.
memorial_us_memorial_day.history: The day grew out of the American Civil War (1861–1865), in which over 600,000 soldiers died. In May 1868 General John A. Logan ordered a ‘Decoration Day' on which the graves of fallen soldiers were to be decorated with flowers. The custom spread after both World Wars and today commemorates all U.S. soldiers who fell in war. In 1971 the day was officially moved to the last Monday in May — to create a long weekend.
memorial_us_memorial_day.traditions: At Arlington National Cemetery the President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Families visit graves, decorating them with flags and flowers. At 3 p.m. local time the ‘National Moment of Remembrance' calls for a moment of silence nationwide. There are also traditional parades, barbecues and the Indianapolis 500 motor race.
funFacts: Arlington National Cemetery is the resting place of service members, veterans and eligible family members, not only those killed in war.
The red poppy became a symbol of remembrance after World War I — inspired by the poem ‘In Flanders Fields'.
The first Indianapolis 500 took place on 30 May 1911. Today the race is traditionally part of Memorial Day weekend.
The older name ‘Decoration Day’ refers to decorating graves. The name ‘Memorial Day’ was already in use long before 1971.
memorial_us_memorial_day.imageCredit: Photo: Arlington National Cemetery · Public domain via Wikimedia Commons

memorial_us_patriot_day.intro: Patriot Day is observed in the United States on 11 September in memory of those killed in the terrorist attacks of 2001. It is a national day of remembrance rather than a federal holiday, so schools and offices remain open.
memorial_us_patriot_day.history: On 11 September 2001 hijacked airliners were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York and into the Pentagon, while a fourth aircraft came down in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Thousands of people were killed, among them many firefighters, police officers and other emergency responders. Legislation introduced shortly afterwards by Representative Vito Fossella led to the first Patriot Day being proclaimed for 11 September 2002, and every president since has issued an annual proclamation.
memorial_us_patriot_day.traditions: Flags on public buildings and at private homes are lowered to half-staff, and a moment of silence is observed at 8:46 a.m. Eastern time, the minute the first aircraft struck. Ceremonies take place at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, at the Pentagon and at the Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville, where the names of the dead are read aloud. The date is also observed as a National Day of Service and Remembrance.
funFacts: Patriot Day is a day of remembrance, not a federal holiday, so it is a normal working day.
The New York ceremony pauses six times, marking each impact and each tower's collapse.
Patriot Day is distinct from Patriots' Day, which is marked in April in Massachusetts and Maine.

memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.intro: National Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day is observed in the United States on 7 December. It honours the service members and civilians killed in the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, in 1941, the event that brought the country into the Second World War.
memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.history: On the morning of 7 December 1941 Japanese aircraft attacked the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on Oahu. More than two thousand Americans were killed and many ships and aircraft were destroyed or damaged. The United States entered the war the following day. Congress designated 7 December as National Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day in 1994 under Public Law 103-308; President Bill Clinton signed the joint resolution on 23 August 1994 and issued the first proclamation that November. It is a national observance rather than a federal holiday.
memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.traditions: The American flag is flown at half-staff on federal buildings and at many homes until sunset. The principal ceremony is held at the Pearl Harbor National Memorial in Hawaii, near the USS Arizona Memorial, where survivors, veterans and families gather for a moment of silence marking the time the attack began, a rifle salute and the presentation of wreaths. Similar services take place at veterans' memorials across the country.
funFacts: The observance was created by Public Law 103-308, signed on 23 August 1994; the first official observance was 7 December 1994.
The USS Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor is built directly above the sunken hull of the battleship.
Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day is a national observance rather than a federal holiday, so offices and schools stay open.

memorial_za_human_rights_day.intro: Human Rights Day on 21 March commemorates the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 and celebrates the rights enshrined in South Africa's democratic constitution.
memorial_za_human_rights_day.history: On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a peaceful crowd protesting the pass laws in Sharpeville, killing 69 people. The massacre drew worldwide condemnation of apartheid. After the first democratic elections the day was made a public holiday in 1994, and Nelson Mandela signed the new constitution in Sharpeville in 1996.
memorial_za_human_rights_day.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Sharpeville memorial and Human Rights Precinct, and the government uses the day to promote the Bill of Rights. Communities organise marches, concerts and educational events.
funFacts: The United Nations declared 21 March the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination in 1966, in memory of Sharpeville.
The South African Bill of Rights is considered one of the most progressive in the world.
The Sharpeville memorial lists the names of all 69 victims on individual pillars.

memorial_za_youth_day.intro: Youth Day is a public holiday in South Africa, observed on 16 June. It remembers the Soweto uprising of 1976, when schoolchildren protesting against being taught in Afrikaans were met with police fire, and the many young people who died in the years that followed.
memorial_za_youth_day.history: A government decree required that several subjects in black schools be taught in Afrikaans alongside English, on top of the inferior schooling imposed by the Bantu Education Act. On the morning of 16 June 1976 thousands of pupils marched through Soweto in protest; police opened fire, and unrest spread to townships across the country and continued for months. A photograph of the dying Hector Pieterson, one of the first children shot, carried the story around the world. After the end of apartheid, 16 June became a public holiday in 1995.
memorial_za_youth_day.traditions: The president delivers a national address at a commemoration that moves between provinces each year, and wreaths are laid at the Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum in Orlando West, Soweto, close to where the shooting happened. Schools, youth organisations and municipalities hold marches, lectures and remembrance services, and the whole of June is observed as Youth Month, with programmes on education, work and the rights of young people.
funFacts: The whole of June is observed in South Africa as Youth Month.
The Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum stands in Orlando West, near where the 1976 march was stopped.
The Organisation of African Unity declared 16 June the International Day of the African Child in 1991.

memorial_zw_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day in Zimbabwe is a public holiday on the second Monday of August. It honours those who died in the liberation struggle that led to independence in 1980, together with others later recognised as national heroes.
memorial_zw_heroes_day.history: Zimbabwe's independence in April 1980 followed a long armed struggle against white minority rule in Rhodesia, known in Zimbabwe as the Second Chimurenga. Fighters and civilians died in large numbers over more than a decade of conflict. After independence the new state set aside a day each August to remember them and built the National Heroes' Acre on a hillside outside Harare as the burial place for those granted national hero status. The holiday is immediately followed by Defence Forces Day on the second Tuesday of August.
memorial_zw_heroes_day.traditions: The main ceremony takes place at the National Heroes' Acre in Harare, where the president lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and addresses the nation. Provincial and district heroes' acres hold parallel ceremonies, families visit graves to lay flowers, and church services and veterans' gatherings are held. State broadcasters carry the Harare ceremony live, and a commemorative gala is often staged nearby.
funFacts: The National Heroes' Acre stands on a hillside a few kilometres from central Harare.
Heroes' Day is followed the next day by Defence Forces Day, giving two linked public holidays.
Burial at the National Heroes' Acre is reserved for those formally granted national hero status.

memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.intro: On 8 May, Europe remembers the end of the Second World War on the continent in 1945 and the millions of people who died in the war, in occupation and in the camps.
memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.history: The unconditional surrender of the German armed forces was signed in Reims on 7 May 1945 and again in Berlin-Karlshorst on 8 May, taking effect late that night. Many countries, among them France, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Ukraine, mark 8 May as a day of remembrance or a public holiday; in Germany it has been described as a day of liberation since a much-quoted speech by Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker in 1985. The United Nations designated 8 and 9 May as days of remembrance and reconciliation for those who lost their lives in the war.
memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.traditions: Wreath-laying ceremonies take place at war memorials, tombs of the unknown soldier and former concentration camps, often with a minute of silence and the reading of names. Veterans, officials and schoolchildren attend; flags fly at half-mast in some countries and at full mast in others that mark the day as a liberation. Survivors and their descendants share memories in schools and memorial sites.
funFacts: The surrender took effect at 23:01 Central European Time on 8 May 1945, which was already 9 May in Moscow.
The war in the Pacific continued until Japan surrendered in August and September 1945.
In Berlin the 8 May was a one-off public holiday in 2020, the 75th anniversary.

memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.intro: Le 24 avril, les Arméniens du monde entier se souviennent des victimes du génocide de 1915 dans l'Empire ottoman, au cours duquel environ 1,5 million d'Arméniens ont perdu la vie.
memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.history: Le 24 avril 1915, des centaines d'intellectuels et de dirigeants communautaires arméniens furent arrêtés à Constantinople, événement qui marqua le début des déportations et des massacres. L'Arménie observe officiellement cette journée depuis 1988 et elle est devenue un jour férié après l'indépendance.
memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.traditions: Des centaines de milliers de personnes se rendent au mémorial de Tsitsernakaberd à Erevan pour déposer des fleurs autour de la flamme éternelle. Des services religieux, une minute de silence et des concerts du souvenir ont lieu dans toute l'Arménie et la diaspora.
funFacts: Le mémorial de Tsitsernakaberd a été inauguré en 1967 ; ses douze dalles de basalte symbolisent les provinces perdues de l'Arménie occidentale historique.
Le myosotis est devenu le symbole officiel du centenaire en 2015 et est toujours porté aujourd'hui.
Plus de 30 pays ont officiellement reconnu les événements de 1915 comme un génocide.

memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.intro: Le 24 mars, Journée de commémoration pour la vérité et la justice, marque l'anniversaire du coup d'État militaire de 1976 en Argentine et rend hommage aux victimes de la dictature qui a suivi.
memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.history: Le 24 mars 1976, les forces armées ont renversé la présidente Isabel Perón et ont gouverné jusqu'en 1983. Au cours de ces années, environ 30 000 personnes ont été kidnappées, torturées et « disparues ». Cette journée a été créée par la loi en 2002 et est devenue un jour férié en 2006.
memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.traditions: Les organisations de défense des droits de l'homme, en particulier les mères et grands-mères de la Place de Mai, mènent une grande marche vers la Place de Mai à Buenos Aires. Les écoles dispensent des cours de mémoire et de démocratie et d'anciens centres de détention comme l'ESMA ouvrent leurs portes.
funFacts: Le foulard blanc des Mères de la Place de Mai, à l'origine une couche lavable, est devenu le symbole de la recherche des disparus.
Les grands-mères de la Place de Mai ont identifié plus de 130 petits-enfants nés en captivité.
« Nunca más » (Plus jamais ça) est le titre du rapport de 1984 de la commission vérité et la devise du jour.

memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.intro: Le 2 avril, l'Argentine se souvient des soldats qui ont combattu et sont tombés lors de la guerre de 1982 aux Malvinas (îles Falkland) et rend hommage aux anciens combattants.
memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.history: Le 2 avril 1982, les forces argentines débarquèrent sur les îles, dont l'Argentine revendique la souveraineté depuis 1833. La guerre de 74 jours avec le Royaume-Uni a coûté la vie à 649 Argentins et 255 Britanniques. Cette journée a été instituée en 2000 et est devenue un jour férié en 2001.
memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.traditions: Des cérémonies ont lieu au Monument aux morts à Malvinas, sur la Plaza San Martín à Buenos Aires et dans les villes de tout le pays. Défilé des anciens combattants, les drapeaux flottent en berne le matin et les écoles rappellent l'histoire des îles.
funFacts: Le monument de la Plaza San Martín répertorie les noms des 649 Argentins tombés sur des dalles de marbre noir.
La plupart des conscrits n'avaient que 18 ou 19 ans.
Le cimetière de Darwin, sur les îles, abrite les tombes de 237 soldats argentins ; les familles peuvent lui rendre visite depuis 1991.

memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.intro: L'Argentine commémore la mort du général José de San Martín, libérateur de l'Argentine, du Chili et du Pérou, décédé le 17 août 1850 en France.
memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.history: San Martín a dirigé l'armée des Andes à travers les montagnes en 1817, a aidé à libérer le Chili et a proclamé l'indépendance du Pérou en 1821. Il a passé ses dernières décennies en exil en Europe. Ce jour férié a été créé en 1938 et est déplacé vers un lundi pour former un long week-end.
memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.traditions: Des couronnes sont déposées dans son mausolée de la cathédrale métropolitaine de Buenos Aires, gardé par le régiment de grenadiers à cheval qu'il a fondé. Les écoles mettent en scène des pièces de théâtre et chantent la « Marche de San Lorenzo ».
funFacts: San Martín est connu comme le « Père de la Nation » et apparaît sur de nombreux billets et pièces de monnaie argentins.
Sa dépouille fut ramenée de France à Buenos Aires en 1880.
La traversée des Andes a couvert des cols supérieurs à 4 000 mètres avec environ 5 000 soldats.

memorial_au_anzac_day.intro: L’Anzac Day, le 25 avril, honore les Australiens et Néo-Zélandais qui servirent et moururent dans les guerres, et commémore le débarquement de Gallipoli en 1915.
memorial_au_anzac_day.history: Le 25 avril 1915, l’Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) débarqua à Gallipoli, en Turquie ottomane, pendant la Première Guerre mondiale. Cette campagne meurtrière devint une mémoire nationale fondatrice, et la date commémore désormais tous ceux qui servirent.
memorial_au_anzac_day.traditions: La journée débute par de solennelles cérémonies à l’aube, suivies de défilés d’anciens combattants, de la sonnerie du « Last Post » et des mots « Lest we forget ». On porte des brins de romarin et on joue au two-up, un jeu de pièces traditionnel.
funFacts: ANZAC signifie Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
Les cérémonies à l’aube rappellent le débarquement matinal de Gallipoli.
Le two-up fait partie des traditions de l’Anzac Day. Les conditions dans lesquelles il est autorisé dépendent des règles de chaque État.

memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.intro: La Journée nationale pour la vérité et la réconciliation, le 30 septembre, rend hommage aux enfants envoyés dans les pensionnats ainsi qu'aux survivants, aux familles et aux communautés touchées. C'est un jour férié fédéral depuis 2021.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.history: Pendant plus d'un siècle, environ 150 000 enfants autochtones ont été emmenés dans des pensionnats gérés par l'Église, où beaucoup ont subi des abus et des milliers sont morts. La Commission de vérité et réconciliation a demandé une journée de commémoration en 2015, et le Parlement a créé cette fête en 2021 après l’annonce d’indices de possibles sépultures non marquées à Kamloops.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.traditions: Les Canadiens portent des chandails orange, une coutume lancée par la survivante Phyllis Webstad, dont le nouveau chandail orange lui a été confisqué lors de son premier jour d'école. Les communautés organisent des marches, des cérémonies et des moments de silence, et les bâtiments sont éclairés en orange.
funFacts: La date a été choisie parce que les enfants ont été retirés à leurs familles fin septembre.
La Journée du chandail orange a débuté à Williams Lake, en Colombie-Britannique, en 2013.
Le message du jour est "Chaque enfant compte".
Le dernier pensionnat a fermé ses portes en 1996.

memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.intro: Le 2 août, la République démocratique du Congo commémore les victimes des guerres et des atrocités massives dans l'est du pays depuis 1996, une journée connue sous le nom de « Génocost ».
memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.history: Cette date rappelle le déclenchement de la Seconde Guerre du Congo, le 2 août 1998, dans laquelle furent impliqués plusieurs États africains et d'innombrables groupes armés. Les conflits à l’Est ont coûté la vie à des millions de personnes à cause de la violence, de la faim et de la maladie. Le gouvernement a fait du 2 août une journée nationale du souvenir en 2022.
memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.traditions: Une cérémonie nationale a lieu à Kisangani, ville qui a subi de violents combats en 2000, avec une minute de silence à midi. Les églises organisent des services religieux et des groupes de la société civile organisent des marches et des expositions.
funFacts: Le mot « Génocost » combine « génocide » et « coût » pour indiquer les motivations économiques derrière la violence.
La Seconde Guerre du Congo est parfois appelée « Guerre mondiale africaine » car neuf pays y ont pris part.
Le prix Nobel de la paix Denis Mukwege, médecin de Bukavu, milite depuis longtemps pour la reconnaissance des victimes.

memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.intro: Le 16 janvier, la République démocratique du Congo rend hommage au président Laurent-Désiré Kabila, assassiné à Kinshasa en 2001.
memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.history: Kabila a dirigé la rébellion qui a mis fin au règne de Mobutu Sese Seko en 1997 et est devenu président. Le 16 janvier 2001, il fut abattu par l'un de ses gardes du corps au palais présidentiel. Son fils Joseph Kabila lui succède et conduit le pays vers l'accord de paix de 2002.
memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.traditions: Les cérémonies officielles ont lieu au mausolée de Kabila devant le Palais de la Nation à Kinshasa, où des gerbes de fleurs sont déposées. Ce jour est un jour férié et est souvent marqué avec la commémoration de Lumumba le lendemain.
funFacts: Kabila reçoit le titre de « Mzee », un mot swahili de respect pour un aîné.
Son mausolée à Kinshasa a été inauguré en 2002 et abrite une statue en bronze.
Les 16 et 17 janvier forment ensemble deux journées consécutives de commémoration des deux « héros de l'indépendance » du pays.

memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.intro: Le 17 janvier commémore Patrice Lumumba, premier Premier ministre du Congo indépendant, assassiné en 1961.
memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.history: Lumumba a conduit le Congo à l'indépendance de la Belgique le 30 juin 1960, mais a été renversé quelques mois plus tard lors de la crise du Congo. Il a été remis aux forces sécessionnistes au Katanga et exécuté le 17 janvier 1961 avec la complicité belge, comme l'a reconnu une enquête parlementaire belge en 2001.
memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.traditions: Des cérémonies ont lieu au monument Lumumba sur le Boulevard Lumumba à Kinshasa et dans sa région d'origine. Son discours sur l'indépendance est lu dans les écoles et ce jour est un jour férié.
funFacts: Lumumba n'avait que 35 ans lorsqu'il a été tué.
En 2022, la Belgique a restitué à sa famille une dent coiffée d'or, seule relique restante de son corps ; il a été enterré dans un mausolée à Kinshasa.
Il est considéré comme l'une des figures de proue des mouvements indépendantistes africains et apparaît sur les billets de banque du pays.

memorial_de_june_17_uprising.intro: Le 17 juin commémore le soulèvement populaire de 1953 en Allemagne de l'Est, lorsque plus d'un million de personnes ont protesté contre le régime du SED et ont été écrasées par les chars soviétiques.
memorial_de_june_17_uprising.history: Le soulèvement commença le 16 juin 1953 par une grève des ouvriers du bâtiment à Berlin-Est contre l'augmentation des quotas de travail et s'étendit à des centaines de villes. Les troupes soviétiques ont violemment réprimé les manifestations. En août 1953, l’Allemagne de l’Ouest a désigné le 17 juin comme Journée de l’unité allemande ; il a été observé chaque année jusqu'à la réunification en 1990.
memorial_de_june_17_uprising.traditions: Des couronnes sont déposées sur le mémorial devant l'ancienne Maison des Ministères de la Leipziger Straße à Berlin et sur les tombes des victimes au cimetière de la Seestraße. Le Bundestag et les parlements des Länder organisent des commémorations.
funFacts: Le boulevard menant à la Porte de Brandebourg à Berlin s'appelle depuis 1953 « Straße des 17. Juni ».
Environ 15 000 personnes ont été arrêtées après le soulèvement.
Ces événements sont considérés comme le premier soulèvement populaire contre un régime communiste dans le bloc de l'Est.

memorial_de_november_pogroms.intro: Le 9 novembre commémore les pogroms de novembre 1938, lorsque des synagogues, des magasins et des maisons juifs à travers l'Allemagne et l'Autriche furent attaqués et détruits.
memorial_de_november_pogroms.history: En novembre 1938, le régime nazi organisa une violence généralisée contre les Juifs. Plus de 1 400 synagogues et salles de prière ont été détruites, des magasins et des maisons juives ont été attaquées et environ 30 000 hommes juifs ont été emprisonnés dans des camps de concentration. Les pogroms constituent une escalade majeure de la persécution nazie.
memorial_de_november_pogroms.traditions: Les commémorations ont lieu dans les synagogues et les sites commémoratifs ; dans de nombreuses villes, les gens nettoient les Stolpersteine, de petites plaques de cuivre placées sur le trottoir devant les dernières maisons des victimes, et placent des bougies à côté d'elles.
